==Problem 3==
A Pascal-like triangle has <imath>10</imath> as the top row and <imath>10</imath> followed by <imath>1</imath> as the second row. In each subsequent row the first number is <imath>10</imath>, the last number is <imath>1</imath>, and, as in the standard Pascal Triangle, each other in the row is the sum of the two numbers directly above it. The first four rows are shown below.
<cmath>\large{10}</cmath>
<cmath>\large{10}\qquad\large{1}</cmath>
<cmath>\large{10}\qquad\large{11}\qquad\large{1}</cmath> 
<cmath>\large{10}\qquad\large{21}\qquad\large{12}\qquad\large{1}</cmath>
What is the sum of the digits of the sum of the numbers in the <imath>11</imath>th row? 

<imath>\textbf{(A) } 11 \qquad\textbf{(B) } 13 \qquad\textbf{(C) } 14 \qquad\textbf{(D) } 16 \qquad\textbf{(E) } 17</imath>

==Solution 1==
If we find the sum for each rows (I'll only do the first <imath>5</imath> to illustrate the pattern), we find that row <imath>1</imath> has sum <imath>10</imath>, row <imath>2</imath> has sum <imath>11</imath>, row <imath>3</imath> has sum <imath>22</imath>, row <imath>4</imath> has sum <imath>44</imath>, and row <imath>5</imath> has sum <imath>88</imath>. So we can see that, excluding the first row, the <imath>n</imath>th row has sum <imath>11 \cdot 2^{n-2}</imath>. This means the <imath>11</imath>th row will have sum <imath>11 \cdot 2^9 = 11 \cdot 512 = 5632</imath>. The sum of the digits of <imath>5632</imath> is <imath>16</imath>, so the answer is <imath>\boxed{\textbf{(D) }16}</imath>.

~ToxicWaste

===Why each row is twice the previous row===
Notice that the sum of each row is the slightly different than the normal Pascal's triangle, so the sum of the numbers is similar. Here's a proof of why each number in the normal Pascal's triangle is twice the previous number.
To prove that the sum of each row is <imath>2</imath> times the previous row, use the equation <imath>{(1+1)}^n</imath> with the normal Pascal's triangle and use the binomial theorem from there.

Example: In the fifth row of Pascal's triangle, the numbers are <imath>1, 4, 6, 4, 1</imath>. The first number can be represented by <imath>{4 \choose 0} = 1</imath>, the second by <imath>{4 \choose 1} = 4</imath>, the third by  <imath>{4 \choose 2} = 6</imath>, the fourth by  <imath>{4 \choose 3} = 4</imath>, and the last by  <imath>{4 \choose 4} = 1</imath>. The sum of these five numbers is <imath>16</imath> which is also <imath>2^{4}</imath>. 
Using the binomial theorem with <imath>{(1+1)}^4</imath>, we get <imath>1 + 4 + 6 + 4 + 1 = 16</imath>, the same results in Pascal's triangle. We could also solve <imath>{(1+1)}^4</imath> by converting it to <imath>2^4 = 16</imath>, proving the identity that all rows in Pascal's triangle are exactly twice the previous row and can be represented by <imath>2^{n}</imath>.

~Bros1 (original writer of this on AMC 10A #19)

==Solution 2==
In this Pascal's Triangle-like sequence, after row <imath>2</imath>, each number in row <imath>x</imath> appears twice in the sum of row <imath>x+1</imath>. For example (to illustrate the pattern), the numbers in row <imath>2</imath> are <imath>10</imath> and <imath>1</imath>, and these numbers indeed each appear twice in the sum of the next row (<imath>10, 10+1</imath>, and <imath>1</imath> are the numbers in row <imath>3</imath>, so their sum can be written as <imath>10 \cdot 2 + 1 \cdot 2</imath>). With this pattern, we know that after row <imath>2</imath> the sum of the numbers doubles in each subsequent row, so now by the same calculation as in Solution 1, the sum of the numbers in row <imath>11</imath> is <imath>(10+1) \cdot 2^{11-2} = 11 \cdot 2^9 = 5632</imath>, and thus the answer is <imath>5+6+3+2 = \boxed{\textbf{(D) }16}</imath>.

~Akang11

==Solution 3 (BRUTE FORCE!!!)==
We can write out the first <imath>11</imath> rows with direct computation. Since no calculators are allowed, you will spend at least <imath>5</imath> minutes on this problem, so I do not recommend this way. Here are the first <imath>11</imath> rows.


<cmath>10</cmath>
<cmath>10\qquad 1</cmath>
<cmath>10\qquad 11\qquad 1</cmath>
<cmath>10\qquad 21\qquad 12\qquad 1</cmath>
<cmath>10\qquad 31\qquad 33\qquad 13\qquad 1</cmath>
<cmath>10\qquad 41\qquad 64\qquad 46\qquad 14\qquad 1</cmath>
<cmath>10\qquad 51\qquad 105\qquad 110\qquad 60\qquad 15\qquad 1</cmath>
<cmath>10\qquad 61\qquad 156\qquad 215\qquad 170\qquad 75\qquad 16\qquad 1</cmath>
<cmath>10\qquad 71\qquad 217\qquad 371\qquad 385\qquad 245\qquad 91\qquad 17\qquad 1</cmath>
<cmath>10\qquad 81\qquad 288\qquad 588\qquad 756\qquad 630\qquad 336\qquad 108\qquad 18\qquad 1</cmath>
<cmath>10\qquad 91\qquad 369\qquad 876\qquad 1344\qquad 1386\qquad 966\qquad 444\qquad 126\qquad 19\qquad 1</cmath>

Summing the last row gives <imath>10+91+369+876+1344+1386+966+444+126+19+1 = 5632</imath>. Summing the digits of <imath>5632</imath> gives <imath>5+6+3+2 = \boxed{\textbf{(D) } 16}</imath>.

Edit: After brute forcing two or three rows, it is clear that the sum doubles (<imath>11, 22, 44, 88, \dotsc</imath>), and you can use this to find the sum of the <imath>11</imath>th row as <imath>11 \cdot 2^{11-2} = 5632</imath>, which gives a digit sum of <imath>5+6+3+2 = \boxed{\textbf{(D) } 16}</imath>.

~JerryZYang

==Solution 4 (Fast)==
We can just take the entire triangle modulo <imath>9</imath>, since all the answer choices have different residues modulo <imath>9</imath> and because a number is congruent to its digit sum modulo <imath>9</imath>. Accordingly, since <imath>10 \equiv 1 \pmod{9}</imath>, the triangle just becomes Pascal's triangle modulo <imath>9</imath>, and so by the standard result for the row sums in Pascal's-like triangles, the sum of the numbers in the <imath>11</imath>th row is <imath>2^{11-1} = 1024 \equiv 7 \pmod{9}</imath>. This means the only feasible answer choice is <imath>16</imath>, as it is the only one that is congruent to <imath>7 \pmod{9}</imath>, and so the answer is indeed <imath>\boxed{\textbf{(D) } 16}</imath>.
~Storm1230323

==Solution 5 (Cheese, Gamble)==
We can start brute-forcing the first few rows and figure out the pattern that the sum of the numbers in row <imath>n</imath>, where <imath>n \geq 2</imath>, is <imath>11 \cdot 2^{n-2}</imath>. Now we gamble on this pattern (which is mostly correct for AMC 10 problems) and plug in <imath>11</imath> into <imath>n</imath>, which results in <imath>5632</imath>. Hence the answer is <imath>5 + 6 + 3 + 2 = \boxed{\textbf{(D) } 16}</imath>.

~ROGER8432V3

==Solution 6 (experience) ==
If you failed or sillied the AMC 10 A Question 19, then during the AMC 10 B you gained the experience to know that each row probably doubles in these Pascal-like problems, either in retrospect or during the actual AMC 10 A. 
However, we should probably check, in case you sillied this problem because you didn't check something stupid on the 10 A. 
It is a good decision to check, because we realize that the first row does not conform to the doubling rule, and only the rows right after it do. 
The rest of the solution is similar to how we solve the AMC 10 A Question 19, except less bashy because we only want the sum, not a specific number, and we are given the row number instead of the sum. 
So, we end up getting the sum to be <imath>5632</imath>, and therefore the answer is <imath>\boxed{\textbf{(D) } 16}</imath>.

~vaishnav

==Solution 7 (Generating Function and Combinatorics)== 

We want the sum of the digits of the sum of all entries in the <imath>11</imath>th row of this "Pascal-ish" triangle. We will solve this with far more modular arithmetic than required, even though everything collapses into a simple closed form.

Let the <imath>11</imath>th row be indexed as row \( n = 11 \), with the top row being \( n = 1 \).
Denote row sums by \( S_n \).

Each row begins with <imath>10</imath> and ends with <imath>1</imath>.
For the interior entries, each behaves like a binomial coefficient, but with an appropriate shift, so the entries in row \( n \) looks like:

Row \( n \): \( 10,  \binom{n-2}{1} + 1,  \binom{n-2}{2} + \binom{n-2}{1}, \dots,  \binom{n-2}{n-2} + \binom{n-2}{n-3}, 1 \)

But this is too reasonable, so instead we use generating functions and modular arithmetic.

Define the polynomial for row \( n \):

<cmath>
P_n(x) = 10x^0 + \sum_{k=1}^{n-2} \left(\binom{n-2}{k} \cdot 10 + \binom{n-2}{k-1}\right) x^k + x^{n-1}.
</cmath>

The sum of the entire row is \( P_n(1) \).
So we compute:

<cmath>
P_n(1) = 10 + \sum_{k=1}^{n-2} \left( 10 \binom{n-2}{k} + \binom{n-2}{k-1} \right) + 1.
</cmath>

Break into two sums:

<cmath>
P_n(1) = 10 + 10 \sum_{k=1}^{n-2} \binom{n-2}{k} + \sum_{k=1}^{n-2} \binom{n-2}{k-1} + 1.
</cmath>

We know:

<cmath>
\sum_{k=1}^{n-2} \binom{n-2}{k} = 2^{n-2} - 1,
</cmath>
since it’s the full sum of binomial coefficients minus the \( k=0 \) term.

Also, similarly,

<cmath>
\sum_{k=1}^{n-2} \binom{n-2}{k-1} = \sum_{j=0}^{n-3} \binom{n-2}{j} = 2^{n-2} - \binom{n-2}{n-2} = 2^{n-2} - 1.
</cmath>

So both sums are exactly <imath>\left(2^{n-2} - 1\right)</imath>, but we pretend otherwise and compute them modulo several numbers unnecessarily.

Since we need row \( n = 11 \), compute:

\( n-2 = 9 \).

We now compute powers of <imath>2</imath> modulo various bases, even though we need the exact value.

First:

\( 2^9 = 512 \).

But we do:

\( 2^1 \equiv 2 \pmod{10},  2^2 \equiv 4,  2^3 \equiv 8,  2^4 \equiv 6,  2^5 \equiv 2, \), giving a cycle of length <imath>4</imath>.

Since \( 9 \equiv 1 \pmod{4} \),

\( 2^9 \equiv 2^1 \equiv 2 \pmod{10} \).

This tells us nothing, but we keep it.

Now compute the sums:

<cmath>
\sum_{k=1}^{9} \binom{9}{k} = 2^9 - 1 = 511, \text{ and hence also }
\sum_{k=1}^{9} \binom{9}{k-1} = 511.
</cmath>

Substitute everything:

<cmath>
P_{11}(1) = 10 + 10 \cdot 511 + 511 + 1.
</cmath>

Compute in pieces:

\( 10 \cdot 511 = 5110 \).

Then

\( 10 + 5110 = 5120, 5120 + 511 = 5631, 5631 + 1 = 5632 \).

So the sum of the entries in the <imath>11</imath>th row is:

<cmath>5632.</cmath>

We need the sum of its digits:

\( 5 + 6 + 3 + 2 = 16 \).

Answer:

<cmath>\boxed{\textbf{(D) } 16}.</cmath>

~notvalid
